M. Chaudary/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Pakistan's government says it will challenge a Supreme Court order to move jailed ex-Prime Minister Imran Khan to hospital for medical checks. The country's top court ruled on Tuesday that the 73-year-old be transferred from the Adiala prison in Rawalpindi to the private Shifa International Hospital in the capital, Islamabad, within 48 hours. The ruling "does not fall within the four corners of the law," Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said in a video statement issued on Tuesday night. The minister said a convicted prisoner must be treated inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law, adding that he was requesting Khan's medical tests be carried out at a government hospital instead of a private facility. Concerns of poor health The cricketer-turned-politician has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted on a string of charges that he claims were politically motivated. Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), and his family have repeatedly raised fears about his health in prison and have called for him to be given access to healthcare and visitation rights. His lawyers also say he has lost most of the vision in his right eye . Khan's supporters have staged nationwide protests calling for his release from prison Image: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance Tuesday's Supreme Court order directed authorities to give Khan access to his personal physician. It also said he should be allowed to meet with his family once a week and have a phone call twice a week with his sons who live in London. From PM to prisoner Khan was Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. Following his ouster in a no-confidence vote, he was convicted on a number of charges including allegations of an unlawful marriage and corruption. He was sentenced late last year, along with his wife, to 17 years in prison for graft. Both deny wrongdoing. PTI still enjoys significant support across key provinces in Pakistan, and Khan himself remains a popular figure. His arrest in early 2023 triggered nationwide protests that resulted in hundreds of people being arrested. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Police in riot gear were seen outside the office in Istanbul early on Wednesday By Jaroslav Lukiv ,Â Maia Davies Â and Â Emer Moreau Published 14 October 2026, 07:32 BST Updated 11:50 BST Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channels, halting its live broadcasts. Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and that 11 people had been taken into custody in a raid linked to the channel's owner. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel. It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip ErdoÄan and his government. Halk journalists were initially unable to get into the building, although they later were allowed in, several reporters said on X. There was a heavy police presence in the building, they said. Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday. The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of ErdoÄan's ruling AK party. Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer MahiroÄlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported. MahiroÄlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained. "Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons." The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem ImamoÄlu, widely seen as ErdoÄan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year. Image source, Deniz BayramoÄlu Image caption, A Halk TV staff member shared images of police stood beside a TV studio during the raid ÃzgÃ¼r Ãzel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly". "Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do," he wrote on social media. Ãzel set up the party after being removed as the CHP's leader by a court in May and replaced by a party veteran who had previously been voted out, in a move which further cemented ErdoÄan's grip on power. Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) 2026 World Press Freedom Index , external . The organisation stated that 90% of national media outlets were under government control and criticised the "abusive prosecution" of critical publications in the country, which ErdoÄan has led since 2003. The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship. In September, a court ordered the blocking of access to the website and social media accounts of T24, on the grounds that it had published "LGBT propaganda". In October 2025, the authorities seized control of Tele1, another pro-opposition TV channel, appointing a trustee to oversee broadcasts, which were stripped of all hard-news content. The channel still exists but its pro-opposition stance has been completely neutralised.
